blocks.x: Well you see this instrument, I bought it and I didn't buy it, it was given to me as a present.
How long have you gone, Mr. Martin?

This would be in 1920. This was given to me. I think it's the only left hand instrument, that is, you'll see a sign up at the Tulane, they have a big photograph of a bushy instrument. This is a bushy, see your finger, this is from the left. Now in the ordinary they play from the right. Don't ask me to blow it because I have heart trouble and I'm not supposed to blow on the instrument anymore. Not drink, nothing.
How long did you have played?
Well, before I had this last heart attack I used to sit down and blow a little bit.
Just for yourself?
Just for myself, yeah, you know, just to sit around and blow a little bit on it.
But how long did you play with an actual group of musicians, a band?
Well with bands I've been playing from 1904.
Yeah, but how long, I mean when was the last time though?

In 1938 I reorganized the band. When this music was being taken away from New Orleans, they were calling Chicago Swing. Benny Goodman was in the center then. And what he played, if you look at it, the St. Louis Blues is a copy for my cornet part and also Larry Shields' clarinet part. He had mixed to listen to the records of the original Lixieland Jazz Band when he was only eight years old. And I played, when I first started playing in a group, it would have been about 1904. Most of these groups I played with were the young boys about my age. They played string music and only brass was in the band was me. So I played with one group, I think I would repeat myself, is that all right? No, go ahead. In Long Beach, Mississippi, where we played for dances. There was Henry Young, Joe Jufri, a fellow by the name of Joe DeBarber and myself. Joe Jufri played the guitar and Joe DeBarber was the bass. Henry Young was a talented violinist. He was a learned man. He could play any kind of obelgato or variations when he learned in his books against any melody. Well, at that time I only knew strict melodies, you know, straight melodies. Well, when we come back to New Orleans at Wendor, I joined another group called Tujac Spang. Well, Tujac, he was a butcher in the magazine, Mark and him and his brother played. They one played guitar, one played bass. Henry Young, Fonson Price, who was now a day, played violin, second violin to Henry Young. He was here. But then 1905, 1960, I started learning breakdown. Breakdown was a piece of music that they would call, well, and this man was a little older than I was. Could have been about six, seven years older than me. I could have been about 18, this man was about 25, maybe 26. And the breakdown was this, he started one key, then he got to another key. And when they hit down the B flat on the guitar, which this man played, before he hit down the B flat, he had a breakdown. Now, if you ever fingered a cornet, that you know if you played the instrument on one key and then you try, you're not a good musician. If you tried to play at another key, you'd either have to try to play a little harmony, a little melody, a little something that would come to your mind to fit in with it. Now, it was easy for the string instruments to go down on these different keys because they were playing in easy keys. But I wasn't a learning musician, I was just a faker. And coming up, you know what I mean, I couldn't transpose. If I played in one key, I'd have to play it in that key in that early day, the early stage of the game. And by changing the key, it made me play different things. Well, I started fitting in different little things to the music. And they thought it was great because they were carrying on with the two violins. Henry would play the variations and the other fellow would keep on to the melody. By the time we hit down to the F, by the F key, this fellow would holler, B flat, break down, see? Break down. It was Everybody For Themself. And incidentally, I got a tune called Everybody For Themself. And I later, in my later days, I made this tune, but it's never been made published. But it's copyrighted, and I copyrighted it under an assumed name. And it's called Everybody For Themself. And it's a different rhythm than any I've ever used. I can hum a little bit on here for you. You want to hear it? I'd like to hear it. I'd like to hear it. Da-da-da-da-da-da-da. Da-da-da-da-da-da-da-da. Da-da-da-da-da-da-da-da. Da-da-da-da-da-da-da-da-da. And so on. I have the music. It's copyrighted. In 1921, I had that copyrighted. It's called Everybody For Themself. And it's under the name of Billy Johnson. But it's a copyright owner. It's DJ on the rock. It's my own number.
Why did you do that?

Well, I'll tell you why I did that. The reason I did that, because I had so many numbers on my name. And I had to share with the guys in the band. You understand what I mean? I tried to look out for myself. Up to this time, these fellas rode my back. They composed not only with Shields, who collaborated on some of the numbers. Rager's name is on some of them. But he did nothing but just hold the chords down on the piano, which I gave him to play. Shields collaborated. And on the numbers that Shields collaborated, he's got his name on there. Now, I'm trying to break away from this and get money for myself. I'd seen the handwriting on the wall that some of the fellas wouldn't work. All they were doing was taking the royalties, getting the royalties, contributing nothing to their music. How would you feel? Then I started putting out popular numbers, Summer, Rainy Night. Their name was not on that either. Ramblin' Blues, their name was not on that. Just Shields I, and I had my names on that.
But Shields was a real collaborator. Yes.

Shields collaborated from the beginning. Not from the beginning. I had four tunes out before Shields ever collaborated. But his name was on the Ostrich Walk. But I had them numbers before I left New Orleans. I brought them there. Now, these guys say they played these numbers. Possibly they did. How many bands did I play with? I jumped off this breakdown here. You questioned me. That's how I got to know how to form melodies against a chord construction. And from that on, I was on my own. Now, where was the back on the other side? We were talking about the collaboration of Shields.
Yes.

But that begins in New York. He collaborated on jazz band Ball. On the fidgety feet. And I think, yeah, because the client at Marmalade was one of my numbers. And he collaborated on that. Just he and Regis' name on that. See, because every one of the names on it, the guys were getting jealous. They think that my name shouldn't, their name shouldn't be on that. So I put one of their names on it. And you're bringing me into a place a little ahead of time. But I just want to go on to it now. So, Liverstable Blues. The Ostrich Walks, which was then in New Orleans. I call that Taddy Eagles and that's down. One was named Hunyadi.
Oh, excuse me. Why did you get that name, Taddy Eagles' Nest Down? Did that have anything to do with it?

I thought it was cute to understand. It was hot, you know what I mean? Something, when I blow it down, when I blow this out there, the nest, the bird nesters and things may fall, you know what I mean? Like the kids fool around, I thought something would come down. Because it was such a, I thought it was a good number. Which became one of the pieces mostly copied after in American music. Even down in Time Array. Now we come to that part, the Time Array. I'll let you know how I compose that. And maybe the world will look at me as a man that didn't do nothing but copy. But it wasn't just only copy. If you notice the ending of my tune like I showed you that Negroes use for their background and their thing eight years after us. Da Well now you take the first part of the Tiger Rag. What does it say? Da Now what is that da Did you know what it was? No, you wouldn't know. Na It's a piece of tango. Why did I put it in there? Because being a figure when they asked me for tunes and I didn't know it, I'd blow back at them da That mean to say get over dirty. Oh. Yeah, get over dirty. Just like, wait did you get that hat? That was out before I made mine. But the idea came from those things get over dirty. That was when people, they say this thing was taken from a quadrille. They're wrong. It was taken, I had told you before, the London Bridge. And that's the second part of the Tiger Rag. London Bridge? Yeah. Yeah, in stop time. It's strange ain't it?
And we've got the sheet music for London Bridge but you never have seen the sheet music for the quadrille have you?
No sir, I never seen the sheet music for the quadrille. Have you ever heard of it?

I wouldn't have heard of it. I've never heard of the sheet music for this particular quadrille that Tiger Rag is supposed to be taken from. But we've got sheet music for London Bridge so what does that prove? Well I'll show you how you prove it.

The bridge is falling down. Now you put the stops to it and I'll lay my head on the track of it, idiot. Because I created it. And I know where it comes from. nowhere it comes from. Now we come to the back part, the other part is the riage of the London Bridge. In other words, I could compose too, but I had a simple mind. I was, as they say, elementary. But I had more originality than all these people that live today in this music. Now we come to the last part. We play, I play a melody against John Philip Sousa's, see I'm mixed up, National Angler March. Because these numbers was on the photograph. And I played along with them. Now, the idea comes from the next part. Did you ever hear the German band? Bop, bop. Now elongate those notes and you get, ya, ya. I'll tell you, this is no Negro talking. This is a white man that created this through talking. Not a man that they filled with liquor. I don't have liquor. And I never had needles in my back pocket either. To talk. When you ask me something, I'll tell you where it's come from and how it came about. Now we come to the next part. Hold that tiger. Well, I wouldn't want to put this on tape record. This gentleman says to do it. Well, my place, the I ever composed music, was sitting in the back house. That's where I learned how to play in the toilet. On the toilet. Well, once, during the spring and the winter, my mother used to give us a puddle. I don't think I should put this on there. Go ahead. Go ahead with it?
Sure. Well, nobody will hear this, ya know. We can save it, ya know. And, uh, put it down. Right. Put it down. Right. Put it down.

By blowing the cornet, I was making this. Da, And by forcing, the back part would go. You understand what I mean? I see. And that gave me an idea of putting that into the throat. And I tried to make that on the horn, and I made it on the horn. On the horn. See, on this cornet. Not this one. The one that I had was a little bit. A piece of junk. Now, that's the whole tiger rag in completion. It has a little part of the quadrill. And if anyone says they have it in there, you play the tiger, if you played the tiger rag against what I told you a lot. Da, You see, I wouldn't say this because I put my neck if a good musician heard it. And it ain't gonna be right. But I know where I got it. That good musician can't say that. It's different. Well, I believe that they got it from the quadrill when I see the sheet music. You know, that makes sense. You've never seen it? No, I've never seen the sheet music. No. I'm gonna tell you what it is. It's all lies concocted by a bunch of communists who received money from Russia, the NAACP, Bill Handy, who was a big member of that, and I believe was the star of that. stuff

He wouldn't even play jazz or the blues. He'd committed to paper. This Negro here had went into the hands of the receiver. And I know this tune by the name of Jobo Blues. And I used to play it in the band. And Russell Roberts says to me, you know whose tune that is? I said, no. He says, that's Hannity's tune. I says, it's a damn good tune. I said, let me go and see him. I may be able to record it for him. At that time, he was in the hands of the receiver. I went on over there. And he wasn't there. I spoke to his brother. His brother said, well, go ahead. We agreed on a 10% of the tape. That is, of the recordings that was made. Whatever would accrue to the recordings made by the Dixon Lane Jazz Band. That was agreed on. I recorded the number. And after I recorded it, I got one $50 check. It went around for me. Hold the machine a minute, will you? Uh-huh. Okay, go right ahead.

This is from Handy Brothers Music Company Incorporated. Pace and Handy Music Company. New York, New York, August 1921. Mr. D. James Marocca, the original Dixieland Jazz Band, 147 St. James Place, Atlantic City, New Jersey. Dear Mr. Marocca, we are in receipt of yours at the 2nd, addressed to W.C. Handy, which we have forwarded the same to him. We wish to call your attention to the fact that he is out of the city every since the 16th day of May, and it looks as though he will not return until the last of this month. He has his organization with him, and he is very busy. If you do not hear from him immediately, do not think that your work is not appreciated. I must say that it is a wonderful record, and I think it will be the biggest seller of its kind. When you return to the city, we will be pleased to have you call in to see us at any time. In the meantime, wish to call your attention to the fact that I am sending some orchestrations of your late numbers, which I trust you will make very good use of saying, especially, I like you because you have such loving ways.
Want to read it?
Yeah, what is that?

About Ann Hager's Children's Blues. Wait a minute. Especially, quote, I like you because you have such loving ways. Unquote. Unquote. Ann Hager's Children's Blues. I'm sorry, I beg your pardon. Unquote. Ann Hager's Children's Blues. Unquote. Which are our plug numbers. Can I finish it, Rob?

Give my kindest regards to Mr. Russell Robinson, if he is still with you. With best wishes, we beg to remain very truly yours. Handy Brothers Music Company, Incorporated. P.S. If you have a photograph of the original Dixie Line jazz band, one that I could use for a title cover of St. Louis Blues, would like very, very much for you to rest saying to me so that I could use this for our next issue.
And that's Charles Handy. That's the check. He's the president, Charles E. Handy. That's the check. That's the secretary of treasurer.
And here's a check for $50 from the solvent savings bank and trust company.
And it's like he didn't have sufficient funds.

No, he went into the hands of the receiver. I never bothered him then because I was making $350 a week. It's been said I never did nothing for the colored men, but this will show you what I did for the colored men. And many other colored men that went to follow.
Well, this is a Memphis bank and it's on Charles Handy.

Handy. That's correct. That's where they kept the account. The original name was from Memphis, Tennessee. It was called Pace and Handy, the original friend. Now, this Negro recorded. After Ralph Pell. I think this man runs a southern music company today, if I'm not mistaken. After our big success on Broadway and rising, that was January the 15th, which we opened there. And the sensation we created was something that they had never heard of in 50 years on Broadway. Anyway, the Columbia company, trying to get somebody to compete with us, sent this Ralph Pell to New Orleans where they recorded every white band, every colored band. He found none playing the same music that we played. That's when he went to Memphis, Tennessee. And Handy had a reputation. They had the greatest colored band in the United States at this time. He traveled all over extensively, this colored band, yeah, with his orchestra. I think I played in the last record, one of his records. One of the, on tape, I played you one of his records. And you can see what he played. Now, it said that the Negroes came before us. I've also contradicted that. They came on March the 6th, the great Creole band. If they took the trouble to look up the New York papers, maybe you'll have them in Tulane, you'll have the voice of the deaf. You'll see that I'm telling the truth. And these communistic writers are lying about this jazz business. They were a favor. They stayed there two weeks. Now, this was one of the greatest Negro bands that they had in New Orleans. And the last ad would appear in around December the 27th in Variety. You'll ask me how I remember those things. When a man's gold is as much as I have been, don't take long for him to remember these things. If you've been crucified by a bunch of crumbs, nut men, parasites. I wouldn't call them men. Because if they were men, they would have came and talked to me, seen what I had to offer, then write what they want about me. But today, they tell me I played ragtime. And only in these records you'll find the pristine roots of jazz. They'll say we wanted the creators of this music. They'll say many other things about us. They'll ridicule us. I've been often talked upon as like I was a thief somewhere. That one book had that I think Charles Edward Smith in a book he wrote. He says, yes, the rocker says that the people was astounded at the small amount of musicians. They could get so much music out of it. He meant in a different way. That I had taken other people's music. Well, I have proved that the Negro didn't play this music. In a previous tape that you've taken from me. If anyone's honest and wants to study them things, they'll see where the Negro got their material.
Now, Mr. LaRocco, I want to tell you that we made some tapes Saturday night of Raymond Burke, who used to work with you. You remember?
He didn't work with me. Didn't work with you? No. He played with me once or twice. Yes. I know Larry Burke. You know who Larry Burke is? He's Jules Kazard's nephew. Yes.

And he had some very nice things to say about you and talked about your playing. So you'll be happy to know that other people are backing your story up. If you go to the musicians, some of them will. And Raymond is one of them who will back you up.

Well, Sharky might because Sharky got up and Sharky lost his place in the jazz club by telling the people I was the one who brought this music around the world. Sharky was pulled off a program for the same thing. Now, Sharky was born about eight, nine years old when I was a musician playing music. Sharky wasn't playing music. Harry Shields wasn't playing music. Parenti wasn't playing music. George's Brunessons that they played. They weren't around. But they all got their mouth open big as an alligator trying to get some credit. They did not do them. And I didn't think it was fair. They said, I never give people credit. I have given people credit. I have given Armstrong credit. I have given Big Spider back his due credit. He tried to start a new style. And I'll show you where he got his style. Da-na-na-na-na-na-na-na. I'll reverse that. I can't think of it now what he uses in his thing. Because offhand you get mixed up. It'll come to me after. And many in the licks did. Big Spade. I showed him. He came to me as a school boy when he was 17 years of age. He ran away from home. These people ran a phonograph store. At that time there was only one jazz band. He liked it. Come to see what we looked like. And he come and asked the doorman, could he get in? They looked at him, he was two years old. He said, my daddy plays from the band. He didn't know me or I didn't know him. So he came on up there and he said, Mr. LaRocco, just like he know me. And I had to get him off the floor and I said, sit back here, son. I thought he was a boy from New Orleans. And I let him sit back there. That night I seen he didn't have no place to go. Well, I used to go out most every night and I had a room doing nothing. I told him, you got a place to sleep? He said, no. I brought him to my place and play my carnet all day. Play on the carnet. Asked me to show him different things, which I did. I kept him there a week. And the boys in the band turned and said, Nick, you're doing the wrong thing. You're harboring a minor. You're liable to get in trouble. You understand you better send that kid back home. So I got him, put him on the train. Paid my own money for him. And sent him back to Davenport where he lived. 1923, he comes again. This time he plays. He's playing pretty good corner. He sit in and I let him sit in the band. He played. He played all my numbers. The only numbers he styled himself on. He don't have a place to stand, huh? But he meets a buddy about his own age. I had, Lawrence had quit the band. And this fellow, Jimmy Lytell, had wended. And they formed the Memphis Five, which was a Brooklyn organization. And I had taken out and saw the Seaboy. The Seaboy was about Bix's age and then bummed together. But I had to feed him every day. There was a restaurant called Demi's Restaurant. He could go in there anytime he wanted and get food. And I paid the tab for him. He stayed there about three, four weeks. Then just by loaning the money, go back home. I have letters right here that you can see.
Now, I know you or I, we don't want to take credit away from Bix for what he had. Bix is a great man. Yes.
Bix is a great man.
But also, I'd like to ask you, what are some of the tunes Bix recorded that you remember?

Well, he made Tomlin, blues, many of the Dixieland numbers. Then he did like the rest of them did. Took another tune, rehashed the Dixieland number, and he called it his own. Yeah. All musicians began to get the idea. And the closest that I had seen came to it was the Bob Crosby bunch. They take my fidgeted feet and they called it South Rampart Street Parade. Now, I bet you could play both of them together with only exception in the first part and the last part, the march, the break, the march part, the pudding, because I played . And they played the counter melody to that. And if you listen to them records, you know it, they style it too. Now, they were the only ones that I know that was getting close to what I used to do in a big scale. They took this Maryland, but there was nuts, because that had no part of Maryland. Maryland should have been with its own harmony, but they added a tune to themself that Leo Feist made money on it, and they got nothing. You understand what I mean? I don't know who created that part, but that's a different tune.
What did they call it? They called it Maryland.
They were staples that. You understand the story? My Maryland, my Maryland. Yes, I see. Then the cland of that would go .
And Feist issued this what?
Correct. Maryland. He did. A new arrangement on Maryland. They got exactly nothing. Anyone. Listen. If you take the time around. . . .
I got ideas, these men, certainly I wasn't the only one, jada, jada, jada, jada, jingle dee, and all comes from the same kind of stuff. These tunes came after.
Well what about the bands in the late 1910s and the early 20s?
Well they all played right after they heard you on music. Wait a minute, 1910?
1910s, in the late 1910s, you know, 1918.

Well now, the bands, they played regular popular tunes. I never heard any numbers that was improvised or worked on. If they played a chorus of different tunes, they may have had a little bit flourishes to it with their own. I don't say they didn't do that, but they were playing ragtime. I played ragtime. And the rhythm wasn't changing until I hit Chicago. Now this is going to be a strange thing and this is why they say the miracle couldn't happen. There was a dance team called, wait a minute, the castles. And at the castles was bringing out a new dance, like a straight dance, like a walk. Now ragtime music would fit it. But I noticed the general public. It was hard for them with the methods of music we were playing, that jumping music. So I decided to play in march time. Slow down, making a fast stride out of it. Fast, making a fast march. Instead of the four beats, it was customary, it was playing around New Orleans. We made two beats and a syncopated beat. That's what give it the drive and qualities. Now the musicians that came up from New Orleans, they still would play in ragtime. Many of them followed us up to Chicago. I named them any of the bands. Brown come back the second time, he was still a failure. They had Johnny Fisher's band, he's still a failure. New Orleans band, he was still a failure. Who's that?
New Rock, Freddie New Rock. Yes.
New Rock, Freddie New Rock. Go right in here. There was Judy Stevens, Rag Baby Stevens, and the Berenson brothers. What were their names? Doc Berenson and Benny Berenson. I don't know Doc's name.
Well that's good enough.

He stayed up in Chicago and taught music. Now most of these guys outside of one or two were note readers. And the note readers couldn't play even good ragtime. Like the boys in New Orleans played, they played a little bit different than the note readers played. But that didn't stop them from coming to Chicago. They came, but no band drew the crop. They came, but they went to the Shilly Cafe. It was here. After the first few set of dances, I seen the people, didn't like the music. They liked it, it was a little different, but it didn't pep them up. I began to say, well we're going to take the railroad tracks and walk home. That's a hard long walk, a thousand miles back to New Orleans. I began to watch their feet move. Now maybe they'll dispute me on this. I was one of the best dancers that they ever had in New Orleans. And I couldn't give anybody competition on any kind of dance, whether it was the shimmy, whether it was fancy dancing, or the tango, or any other dance. This is taking it a lot of territory. But if many of the boys around New Orleans will tell you, they'll see me dance. And wherever I went, they put a spotlight on me, and I knew dance rhythm. And I watched what these people were trying to do. If you couldn't spin around and make these spins around with this, that kind of music, you'd have to have a smooth music. That was the beginning of jazz music. In the following week or two weeks, the people began calling this music, more jazz, more jazz. Little by little, we caught on, we made a big hit. And only a certain amount of people could come in there. They had a fireman out there. And a policeman. If four people went out the place, four people could come in. Now there was many positions open for the fellows in New Orleans, but they starved to death. Can I tell you what happened to some of them?
Sure.
Well, there was Eddie Rowland came up there. He came up there with Tom Brown on the second try.
Can you give the instruments to the people who want to know?

He played clarinet. Eddie Rowland, after two weeks, they were thrown out of a job. And he was put in jail for no visible means of support. There was only one person he knew. And that was me. Because I happened to be the oldest musician of the bunch that ever went off and played up around out of town. And I had to pay his way out of jail was $25. Put him on a train and sent him back to New Orleans. I have never received one penny from him. He's dead now up to this day. Went in a lock, split business, some way down here in Natchez Alley or somewhere. And he made good at this business. I don't know when he kept his music up anymore. But there were many other boys that came to me for handouts. And I'd help them out. Try to get them jobs. And do everything I could for these New Orleans guys. They couldn't seem to catch the rhythm that we had changed. They thought they played better than me. I was supposed to be a lousers, carnet playing New Orleans. If you hear them talk, they'll tell you about Vega. They'll tell you about Manuel Mello. They'll tell you about Johnny Lala. They'll tell you about Joel Lala. They'll tell you about everybody. But they ain't gonna tell you nothing about Nick LaRocca. They'll tell you about Richard Brulis. You can look up their records and see what they did for this music. Where they went and how far they went. Because of my originality, putting different things in. They thought it didn't belong in the music. I didn't know what I was doing. What I added to the music pleased the people. And they liked it. And whenever I played to an audience. I didn't play to the musicians. I played to the audience. Because they were the paying customers. That's psychology. And I prised myself on trying to be a good businessman in that way. If the tune was too randy. I added too much to it. I'd tone it down. Give them a little more melody. So they could understand it. But after we'd get there three or four weeks. And they heard me play the same tune. Then I'd cut it up. And they'd like it. Because now they have already had a prism of what I was playing. And now they know what I'm playing. But you could not play to a green audience. These harsh numbers that had no melody. Just made out of arrangements. Like they wouldn't understand that music. A musician would. But they didn't. Now many of the boys and the old ones couldn't come in the places where they played. Because they had to sit at the table. They had no money. And they couldn't style themselves. Or on any music. When the four weeks was up at the show. We asked for more money. Well Stein was in the band. So was Nunes at that time. Nunes played more of a melody clarinet. And I was about to get rid of him. And put Shields who had played with me in my early days around New Orleans. Now Shields and I played together all the time. Around New Orleans. About seventh stuff I said, all right, Mr. Rothschild. He sent us to the lawyer. Sam had already taken an injunction to keep us from working. So I went to the lawyer and explained the case. And we didn't have to copy the contract. So the case came up the next day because it was an emergency. This lawyer had prevailed upon the lawyer to hear our case, see what I had to say. So the lawyer instructed me what to say. And here's what the words this man told me. Your Honor, we throw ourselves on the voice of the court. If we're not allowed to work, we have no way of a livelihood, and we become a public charge on the city of Chicago. So the judge asked Sam Hare, lawyer. Sam Hare did not appear in court. The lawyer was there to represent him. We had 20 more weeks contracted, $25 a week. We couldn't live on that. Room rent was $12 a week. I was married and had to send money home. Didn't have no money to send home. How was we to live? We would have stomped to death. So when the lawyer got up there, the judge looked at the contract and said, there don't specify no hours in there. He says, till closing time. Now, what is closing time? They asked me. I said, we work from 8 o'clock sometime or 5 o'clock the next morning. The judge looked at him and said, I thought slavery times is over. Case dismissed. You boys go get yourself another job. Good luck to you. Hold that wire. We went over to work for Mr. Rothschild. I'm going to hear my story. Stein did not want to come with the van. He stayed there at the Shelling Cafe at $25 a week. When I used to get on the floor and dance over there and pick up about $10, $20, we would have to split it with entertainment. Two girls, singers, a man singing a piano player. Now, whatever they collected, they kept for themselves. We were forced to split with them. I thought that was an unfair division because the people were giving it to the band and not to them. Well, that was one of our complaints. The next complaint, we didn't have enough money to live on, even with these collections, because room rent was so high in Chicago and each was high. We were maintaining two homes. So Mr. Rothschild gave us the job. So we used the Chicago term of there by the name of Royal Carter. Now, this is one of the changes against in the band. The first band, I forgot to tell you the name of the first band. When we went to Chicago, we had no name for the band. Five names was put in a hat. Stein's name came out. It was called Stein's Dixie Band. Later, when the people started calling our music jazz, Harry James Billis' jazz band. At the Del Abbey Cafe, we didn't decide on any name at all. We worked there four weeks, two weeks with Earl Carter until Spobara came up from New Orleans.
What was his name again? Carter?

Earl Carter. Yeah. A Chicago drummer. He filled in for two weeks. And Spobara comes up and takes his place. This man knew that that's all the way we used him for two weeks. And we did pretty good at the Del Abbey. Then Harry James buys an entrance in the Casino Gardens with Aikenbar and Reeves. And he approaches us and offers us $75 a week to play in the Casino Gardens. We went and played the Casino Gardens. That was Kinzen Clock. And that band was Spobara. Nunes was still with us. And Edwards, Regas, and myself. Well, this man on the Clarence, he liked to drink, mix with the people. And you can't go anywhere doing that, mixing with the patrons of the place, drinking with them, sitting at the table. And every time he'd want them to put you in a mind of some bordello, you'd have to give them a signal for them to come and play. So I got mad at him. And I had heard from Shields. And I had sent Shields money to come to Chicago. Then I give this man his two weeks' notice. That was about the second or third week that we played at the Shields Cafe. We started there around... It only was in one band And that was in the original Dixieland Jazz Band That takes a lot of ground But let them prove to me where they worked Any place that they worked that they made a success It's feat that has been unequaled by any musical organization or act to this day I believe I told you the change of Nunes being changed in Shields Now that's the second change in the band After Rides & inch horn That is the diameter of the outside horn The horn could have been about three foot long And it was eight inches in diameter And out of that came a little horn about four inches in diameter Where Larry was to play And I stood back about 20 to 25 feet The drummer was alongside of me He was not supposed to use the bass drum because it would break up the wax Or the matrix Dig holes in it And ruin it All he could play was in between like You know like the licks in between He could do that And he played mostly on the kettle drum And on the wood blocks and bells Now this is the hardest way in the world of playing music Of having musicians separated Because when musicians are put together like they record today You can feel one another You can almost know what the other man is going was about 15 feet from the horn And Larry stood about four feet from his little horn And the piano was facing me Direct under the horn Now they had a white light A white light was going And that's when they changed You're supposed to watch the light up there And the red light would come on And each man was the count mainly two And we started It's beyond me How we ever started together I don't know But it looks like God was with us Because we always started together I was in the back of them They could hear me But I couldn't hear them Now there was no way of me I've thrown in an extra lick and easy as he wants And in the booth this man raises the volume up

to make it equal to the other. There was no reason of volume here. You hear the cut or be cut down with the Dixieland Jazz Band. And I believe that's what gave us the edge on all of it because there was no time that I'd ever have to take down on any record record when it went 12 hours. I could still hold that heart in my mouth and play it. Now this might be bragging, but I did it many times. Till the dancers toppled over, I'd stayed in playing. One after the other, until the manager was making stuff. That's the kind of clientele we had at Rice with us. They were all rich people. They liked it. They went for it. how many times would you cut a tune? I'll put it that way, because I can't pronounce anything.

Well, we'd play a test record over once. See what I mean a test? And then go through that. Then we'd start on a real matrix. We may make two, three, sometimes four. They didn't issue them till May, till the Liber Stable Blues became a national hit. It was all over the world, even down in Honolulu. And all the way the American forces went, they were carried overseas by the American troops, which we entertained over a million men. I had pastors to every fort and every hospital in New York. And we entertained the soldiers and sailors. I played on the bills with Caruso. I played on the bills with Jolson. I played on bills with Eddie Cantor. In fact, Eddie Cantor used to work downstairs in the Kidder Review for Gus Edwards. I played with Red Heart Mama, what's her name? Sophie Cousin. No. Yeah, I played two times with the same boss with her, but not with her. I played once at Rideswell. It was in 1919 when she was supposed to come in the fourth of 400 room. And they put her into Paradise and left her, stayed there until our time to go to England. See? Those people were good to us because we made business for them. We made fortune for them. They never got a cover charge before until the Dixon Land Jazz Band, where they got a dollar a cover. They paid nothing to us. We earned money for them. They didn't pay anything to us. They made money, made a fortune on us. You had to pay a cover and have a card to come in there. In other words, you was a member of the 400 Club. That was exclude the riff raff and the cheap customers out. Because the more popular music was getting, the more the riff raff was coming to get in on it. So they formed a club. You would have to have a card to get in. You would see that in the file, there were a card in there. And where was that? Well, Mae West. She was one? I played on Bill. Sure, I got him right in there. He in there. When you go to them things, you'll say, I played with Eva and Billy Galleang. She came here. She's not from New Orleans. They give a great big spill in the paper. I'm a poor little digger boy on the other side of the tracks. I was headlining on the same bills with her. They didn't even know me. They didn't know who I was. I came back here in 1925. Nobody even noticed me. I never looked for notoriety. I never looked for nothing. I never looked for credit for nothing. I never went anywhere. I came here as a sick man. I had a nervous breakdown. I came here for my health. I hadn't made a lot of money. I came here almost at $100,000. The other boys didn't have that much because they used to go spend as with women. Run around here and there and spend it. And I saved mine. Because coming from a poor family and knowing there was only one opportunity in my life to make it. I was to make this one opportunity. The old addicts say, opportunity only knocks once. And I made the best of it. And I have it. I'm skipping the game. I'd like to tell you when Regis died, or before Regis was sick, that we had trouble getting a piano player to play the rhythm. The first time Billy Hollander, who had heard us for two years in an orchestra in the next room from where we played in Rines. He sat in there about four days until we had Harry Shields to come up. Who was the brother? Larry Shields.
Eddie Shields.

Eddie Shields. Eddie Shields. Eddie Shields. Harry's a clarinet. Yeah. Eddie Shields. Eddie Shields. He was older than Harry. And he came on up there and he couldn't fit into the rhythm. We kept him two weeks to make enough money to go back home. We tried on every song platter. We wouldn't go to London England. I had already signed a contract with the Morris Agency. We'd go to London to open the Joy Bells Theater. And out of a clear sky after trying to bounce, you know, I had Sidney Lansfield sit in the band. Today he's a big movie executive. Now you know I'm not going to say this because that man could sue me, but he played with me two weeks and he couldn't make the grades. Sidney Lansfield. He's out in Hollywood somewhere. He's a big movie magnet today.
And, uh, I hate to ask this. This is embarrassing to him, I know, but what did you require of a piano player that he couldn't play?

They could not play the rhythm. I see. They couldn't get the rhythm. As simple as you think it was, not even Al Menard who was the greatest piano player on the American stage. He couldn't fit with us. He disrupted the band. Each one of them, they played a different kind of rhythm than we played. It was not until the records come out that these fellows began to decipher and know what our success was from the rhythm.

Play chords and he played bass, played bass and contramelody. We were able to fill in. In other words, he'd have to know the rhythm twice, play the chords, and he played bass too. You see, there was bass hand. And the other one he played, contramelodies, no melody. All contramelodies and harmonies. And that's what he was to play. And I couldn't get to these fellows. All they played bird music up on top of the piano. Bird music. There was no foundation tone and they disrupt the band. Now, along comes Robinson. He comes in the hotel. I was staying at that time at the Pontchartrain Hotel, now called Wilson Hotel. They have changed the name again. That was in the back of Ryzenweather. He heard that from going around the music publishing, he heard we needed a piano piano. And I said, yeah. I said, can you feel it? He says, I think I can. He says, me and my brother was going around to picture shows as an added attraction. Playing in the picture shows along with your records. I played the piano, my brother played the drums. And he used to think it was a whole band. We had a great big photograph, a great big heart on it. And that's how he learned the tunes. I went over to Ryzenweather's that afternoon with him. And I heard him play. He played it better than anybody that I'd ever heard play before. I says, all right, you want the job? I said, yeah. But he filled in for Ryzenweather's two theater jobs we had. One was in Brooklyn, one was in New York. And we leave for London, England. When we got to London, England.

Oh, yes. Edwards was drafted around, in the middle, almost in fall. We came to New Orleans to get a trombone player. Emil played connet. He had been with several bands up to Chicago. His parts was copied from Edwards' trombone part. Now you don't have to believe me to take the records that Emil played. Take the records that Edwards played and you'll see that he's got the trombone parts of Edwards.

I don't want to be rude. That's where that idea comes. I had told Mr. Howard Jacobs that's where this tune was born. He in turn laughed at it. But I'm telling you the truth of the tune. Where the tunes come in, my inability as a gifted musician, only having a few little ideas about me to put to use the different parts and make a number. I'll tie you on the cuff. I'll tie you on the cuff. I'll tie you on the cuff. Here we go. Howard Jacobs is a man who writes Remmelade. He was sent here by the Newsweek people to find out if I was still living. The Newsweek people must have seen all this Negro propaganda and writings. And they sent Howard Jacobs to find out if I was wrong. Howard Jacobs must have the letter in his possession yet because he showed it to me. And that's how Remmelade, he wrote this story, Jazz Prophet Without Honor in his own hometown. And I explained to him where this tune was composed. I was elementary, that's true. I had no learning on that one. Just like a fake or a gypsy would have to find how to make different things. And I was so on my own that I couldn't read music. I had to find new methods of making new tunes. And that's how these tunes come about. Because every number that I have, I can prove to you the source where it came from. And the idea how it was arrived at. Let's go. Whoa, whoa, whoa. Okay, it's working now. Go ahead. When our first record came out, or before our first record came out, it was called Lyrics Table Blues. Mr. King of the Victor Company thought that the title suggested and asked us to change it to Barnyard Blues. We had the name, the title of the tune changed. It was copyrighted. The man who had his numbers copyrighted was our manager, Max Hart. He copyrighted a number under his name. Also, the copyright owner was under his name. This record was released. And when the Victor Company put it out, it was Lyrics Table Blues. Al C. Nunez, who had been my first client editor in Chicago, he told this Roger Graham that was his tune. They looked it up. And they found that we didn't have the copyright on the Lyrics Table Blues. So, Wood Kelly, Roger Graham, Nunez, and Wilcox. The client player, the cornet player of Brown's Band. They went into Sherman Hotel, and they got some men to take this down in notation. And they published this tune, Lyrics Table Blues. I had taken an injunction against them. And when we went to court, the question wasn't on the Lyrics Table Blues. They said, I rehashed this tune from the Morpah Blues. And the Morpah Blues is supposed to be owned by Lopez. My lawyer didn't know, I didn't know music. I couldn't explain how this thing came about. They said it was the same chord construction. But the lawyer didn't take in mind that this tune that they'd taken off the record was the Lyrics Table Blues. It was the same tune I had played on the record in comparison with the Barnyard Blues. They were bringing in another tune that they had no music to, and said it was the same tune. So, the judge said there's so much lying in the case on both sides that he put the thing in public domain. There was nothing to the tune. And in your two-inch files, you'll find this article of the judges, the witnesses and all. And the witnesses packed. Now, when I play you the Lyrics Table Blues, and I'll play you this other tune, let any musician tell me that they're alike. Now, there's one difference in them. I want to explain to you. The reason I call it the Moaning Blues, because when I got back to New York, Mr. Booker wanted to take it to High Court, because he said that they were not talking on the merits of the Mopah Blues, they were talking on the merits of being similar to the Lyrics Table Blues, which they had copied from the record. And my piece that I had played on the record, and he said, certainly there must have been some comparison. He said it was a miscarriage and a thing. And he wanted me to take it to High Court, and he guaranteed me win. I said, well, how much it would have cost? He says, it would cost you about $350 to $500 to Mr. Booker. He said, well, I'm taking the suit against Victor, and you won't put a nickel off him. He says, you do what you want. So he had me to sign the papers. We sued Victor for $10,000, because in those two-line files of Cedar letters, where Victor Havinson changed his title to Barnyard Blues. And we sued, Mr. Booker sued him for $10,000. In one week, they settled for $2,500, and give us a contract for 10 more numbers. Now, I'll play the Liverstable Blues for you first. Wait, I ain't got some needle in there. Okay. Got the needle fixed and everything. 된 stuff with Thank you. And I'm going to prove to the public how wrong they were.

Now if there's any man living that knows anything about the Mopah Blues, which was played in New Orleans ten years before I went to Chicago, they'll attest to this tune when they hear it. With the exception of the introduction and the runs. The runs were made purposely so whoever on this tune could cry to sound something like the Liverstable Blues. Now we won the suit, we got the royalties from the Liverstable Blues, from the Victor people, and we are next to peace which I'm sorry to say that I didn't want. But Mr. Boyk had told me go ahead, that's the only way we can show the court now. If the man come forward and claim this peace, then all that money that we had put out would have to be rescinded to us. Now here it is here. Now this court is my own adding to it. It had nothing new with the Mopah Blues. Now this is the Mopah Blues. Now this is the Mopah Blues. Now this is the Mopah Blues. Now this is the Mopah Blues. Now this is the Mopah Blues. Now the Indian didn't go like this. It went something like the Mopah Blues. This was not into their thing. This I added to make them cry. I added to make them cry. I added to make them cry. The Mopah Blues. Thank you. And they find out about it, they'll think that I've lied all the way through. That's why I give you this, for your take. I'd like to bring you up to the time that we went to London. After Robinson joined the band, we boarded the steamship.
Now I want to interrupt you again. These things are, to me, important to bring up. Now you made records for Victor and Columbia before you went.

Overseas, and Aeolian too. It was at this time that we had friction with Victor, that we went over to the Aeolian company. And we didn't know the Aeolian had a different soundtrack. We thought that they'd play on any machine. And we went over there on a royalty basis. That'd give us two cents a royalty, like they give Caruso and them, for the records. So we made several records for them. But when they found out, I think they had either the Hillingdale or the Laracut, I couldn't tell you. Because I don't know about these things. But you couldn't play them on a record phonograph. You had to get an expansion of something and people wouldn't buy the records. Therefore, that's when we went back to Victor again.
Well, I want to get clear. Who was in the band then, at that time, when you made the records for Aeolian?

All the records that were made in New York, the Aeolian, the Colombian, and the Victor, was the original band and types. Barbara, Shields, Ragus, and myself. And Edwards. That was the original Vixenland Jazz Band. All the masterpieces had been made before Edwards was drafted into the Army.
And we can prove that by checking his Army record then. That's right.

You can prove that from the Army record. I told you we opened it back in Riserwebers around September the 6th. And we played up there. Our contact expired around December the 18th. We were held over, I think, four weeks more until our sailing date. In conjunction with shows, we played around New York City. A couple of the jobs were played with Ragus. In the last two weeks was with Robinson. Then we sailed for England. We arrived in England around April the 1st. We were opening joy bells. And we got into, at Liverpool. We rode a train into London. We got there about 10, 30, 11 o'clock that night. They had no accommodations for us to go. We slept in the girls' dressing room on the long benches that night until they procured rooms for us the next day. And the next day we had to go to police and register. From there, we had to go out and get ration cards. And we were the only band that was allowed to come over there because they thought our kind of music would boost the marl of the British people. We were ridiculed in that show. We opened on the 5th. We played one afternoon and one night.
Go right ahead. You played the show.

We played the show. Before we played the show, we rehearsed in the show. When all the Englishmen laughed at us, the papers carried reports that we was a dog band. Some of them said we was yelping hounds. And they didn't describe our music with anything but was no good. That's the critics in London. And you have a picture that was taken backstage. And all the people sitting down are reporters. That afternoon on the 5th, we opened in the show. We got a fair hand for when the doughboys from the United States Army heard we were in town because we had entertained every one of them that passed through New York. They roughed that show. They crowded the show. That night when we played our numbers, it looked like the roof fell in. George Ruby, who was the head man of the show, along with Albert DeCobble's wife, she was the lead woman in the show, he gave Mr. DeCobble an ultimatum. He says, You take them out the show or I don't go on. Mr. DeCobble had to go out and buy a club to put us in. In the meantime, we worked two weeks in the Palladium. We worked one week up in the north of England. And we came back and opened the 6 and 8 Bond Street Club. We used to name the lady change the Dixie Club. For that contract you have there, we made $200 a week. And 80 pounds extra for every place we played. Extra than the place we were supposed to be. We were cleaning up almost $2,000. That was worth $480, $82, or $83. We stayed there. We finished the contract with him. And they had a clause. If he stayed in there, he didn't have to pay our fair back. In the meantime, I signed the contract with Mitchell and Booker. Rectors at Tottenham Court Road. Now we have, in this band, Robinson, Stillworth, Shields, Bara, Christian, and myself. We go and open that Rectors, on Tottenham Court Road. We made a tremendous success there. Wherever we went, we made a success. And then, on that, he bought a great big place, which was an airplane factory, back in Hammersmith. He signed us up to a six-month contract, with the stipulation that he could put us into another place. And they go to work and remodel this place called the Palli de Dades Hammersmith. And they put us in Hammersmith. Hammersmith's a place, I'd say it was half a block, like you, this way, and almost a square level, 300 feet long, and about 150 feet wide. Now, we have no equipment to help us out. We've grown for playing our instruments, and we feel that harm, that harm. After the week, I jumped there. Robinson, while I was at Rectors, his wife became sick, and he had to return to the United States. He couldn't stand the weather. In his way, Billy Jones, an English pianist, gets into the Dixieland jazz band. Now, here to Florida, I've only went to New Orleans for two different men. Now, this is an Englishman who had heard these recordings, dialed himself on the records, and he played opposite of us in Rectors. And I tried him out for the job, rehearsed it, and he did a good job because some of the records in the English make records, he has played on them, and you'll be able to hear them because if the Tulane gets the records and made it in England, Billy Jones will be on there, and you'll hear he's playing just as good as any American man played because he was styled on the records. In the rhythm. Now, Jones and we played there six months, and after that, he gave us almost another six-month contact, and I didn't renew no more because the pound was falling. He was down to 442, and I didn't want to change the money into American money, and we decided to come back to the United States. Christian came along with me, and when we got back, the war had stopped. Edwards was demobilized out of the Army and had a little band of his own. I don't know what he called his band, but they weren't doing nothing, so I asked you this, you want your place in the band? Because whenever anybody was in the band, they stayed in the band. Like when Edwards was at Rizuela, he was in the Army. I gave him $50 a week out of the money that was collected out of the collection box to help him out. When Ragus was sick, I did the same thing to her. You'll see many numbers in it. When he was in the Army, and Miss Ragus' husband had died, that they're still derived rather to it, for my generosity, of giving them a share and a cut on the records was going to follow. Yet, these people put me down as a thief. When you read Miss Ragus' mail, you'll know different. I took care of them, all of them. I was the only man that knew anything about business in the band. I'd come up the hard way. I only knew one thing, I had to make a success. When we went to Paladin Dance, we played a few sets there. We had 5,800 people on the opening night. So I started playing some English numbers that they knew over there, like, I can't think of the numbers now, was Cole Porter's number. I never realized, da-da-da-da-da-da-da. Oh, they liked that kind of stuff. And then many others, like, I got my captain working for me now in different popular tunes, and every now and then I'd slap them one of these snot balls that I had. You understand? That's all I call them, but today they classed me as a great composer. I've looked upon myself as nobody. Just a man was a figure, put these things together. And I was before the rest of them, and they followed me. we played there, we made a huge success. And if you'll see in there, when...
The man offered me jobs to come back. I had jobs for Paris. And I came back to New York in 1920. I left English piano player. Can we stop now? Yeah.

segments.title: La Rocca's left-handed cornet and his heart condition
segments.summary: He explains the cornet was a 1920 gift, is left-handed, and that heart trouble now stops him playing except at home.

segments.title: First bands from 1904, breakdown playing, and the 1938 revival
segments.summary: He recalls playing with string bands in Long Beach and New Orleans from 1904, learning to fit melody to changing keys, and copyrighting Everybody For Themself under a pseudonym.

segments.title: Copyrighting under his own name and Shields's collaboration
segments.summary: He explains he put tunes under his own name because bandmates took royalties, and discusses Shields as collaborator.

segments.title: How La Rocca says he composed Tiger Rag
segments.summary: He explains Tiger Rag as built from a tango figure, London Bridge, a Sousa march and a German band, and disputes the quadrille origin.

segments.chapter: Handy, Bix and disputes over credit
segments.title: W. C. Handy, Jobo Blues, and the letter and check
segments.summary: He tells of recording a Handy tune on a 10% royalty deal, and Allen reads Handy's letter and a $50 check that was not honored.

segments.chapter: Handy, Bix and disputes over credit
segments.title: Handy, Columbia's search, and his rebuttal of Negro priority claims
segments.summary: He argues white bands came first on Broadway, cites the Creole band's visit, and attacks critics of his claim.

segments.chapter: Handy, Bix and disputes over credit
segments.title: Raymond Burke's tapes
segments.summary: The interviewer says Raymond Burke praised La Rocca; he says Burke played with him only once or twice.

segments.chapter: Handy, Bix and disputes over credit
segments.title: Giving credit and the young Bix Beiderbecke
segments.summary: He says others resent him, and tells how a teenage Bix came to him in New York, stayed and returned in 1923.

segments.chapter: Handy, Bix and disputes over credit
segments.title: Bix's repertoire and the Bob Crosby band copying his tunes
segments.summary: He says musicians rehashed Dixieland numbers and the Bob Crosby band copied Fidgety Feet and Maryland, with Feist profiting.

segments.title: Bands of the late 1910s and the change to march-time rhythm
segments.summary: He says other bands played ragtime and that he changed the rhythm in Chicago after seeing the Castles' dancing.

segments.title: New Orleans bands failing in Chicago and the Schiller Cafe
segments.summary: He names New Orleans bands that failed in Chicago and describes how dancers' response made jazz at the Schiller Cafe.

segments.title: Eddie Rowland, playing to audiences, and the Stein contract lawsuit
segments.summary: He recounts bailing out Rowland, his audience approach, and the court case ending the Schiller contract with Stein, leading to Rothschild and the band name.

segments.title: Drummers and the Casino Gardens job
segments.summary: Earl Carter fills in for Sbarbaro, and Harry James offers $75 a week at Casino Gardens.

segments.title: Schiller Cafe to Reisenweber's: the New York sensation
segments.summary: The band gets the name Original Dixieland Jazz Band, goes to New York in January 1917 and becomes a hit at the 400 Room.

segments.title: Imitators and rival bands, and his attack on jazz critics
segments.summary: He names northern bands that copied the ODJB, insists none changed the rhythm, and says only newspapers, not handbills, are proof.

segments.title: Recording for Columbia and Victor, and acoustic recording methods
segments.summary: He describes the failed Columbia session, the Victor sessions with an eight-inch horn, and how many takes were cut.

segments.title: Release of Livery Stable Blues and playing with Broadway stars
segments.summary: The records came out in May, and he describes entertaining troops and sharing bills with Caruso and Jolson.

segments.title: Eddie Shields and Sidney Lanfield fail to fit the band
segments.summary: He describes trying out Eddie Shields and Sidney Lanfield before the London trip.

segments.title: What the band needed from a pianist, and hiring Russell Robinson
segments.summary: He explains pianists had to play bass and countermelody, and says Robinson fit the rhythm.

segments.title: New trombonist replaces Edwards, and unreleased records
segments.summary: He explains how Emil learned Edwards's parts after Edwards was drafted and mentions two unreleased Victor records.

segments.title: Naming Livery Stable Blues and the Max Hart copyright
segments.summary: He explains how the tune was named at Victor and that agent Max Hart copyrighted it in his own name.

segments.chapter: Tiger Rag and Mopah Blues explained
segments.title: Tunes with no names: 'play some dirt'
segments.summary: He says the band called tunes 'dirt', then they briefly discuss the vulgar language.

segments.chapter: Tiger Rag and Mopah Blues explained
segments.title: Disputing Tiger Rag claims and explaining its sources again
segments.summary: He rejects the Lomax-found claimant and again breaks down Tiger Rag, with Howard Jacobs's Newsweek visit.

segments.chapter: Tiger Rag and Mopah Blues explained
segments.title: The Mopah Blues lawsuit over Livery Stable Blues
segments.summary: He says Livery Stable Blues echoed an older tune, that they won the royalty suit, and plays the Mopah Blues.

segments.title: Aeolian Vocalion records and who played on them
segments.summary: He explains the move to Aeolian over royalties, the playback incompatibility, and the lineup on the New York records.

segments.title: Reisenweber's return and sailing to England
segments.summary: He gives dates for the band's return, last jobs and arrival in England.

segments.title: The London show, the dog-band reviews and the Dixie Club
segments.summary: He describes critics' mockery, the troops' response, the Dixie Club contract and his return to New York in 1920.
